slides.title: Quick check before we dig in

interaction.hint: Only one of the four moves can turn a shape into its mirror image.

config.prompt: A triangle is moved, and its image is the same size but faces the opposite way round, like the view in a mirror. Which move was it?

options.whyWrong: A rotation turns the shape but never produces a mirror image. The corner labels still run round the shape the same way.
A translation only slides the shape along. It cannot make the shape face the other way.
An enlargement changes the size, and this image is exactly the same size as the object.

config.successText: Only a reflection produces a mirror image. Spotting a flipped shape is exactly how you will recognise reflections on the paper.

interaction.hint: Subtract: image minus object. The order matters.

config.prompt: A point $(2, -1)$ has been translated to $(-3, 4)$. The column vector is...

options.whyWrong: You did object minus image. Always image minus object.

config.successText: $(-3 - 2,\ 4 - (-1)) = (-5, 5)$. Image minus object, always.

altExplain.prompt: Subtraction trick. The vector is always (image minus object). Top: $-3 - 2 = -5$. Bottom: $4 - (-1) = 5$. Vector: $\begin{pmatrix} -5 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$.

slides.title: Enlargement: centre and scale factor
slides.prompt: An enlargement is defined by two things: the point it scales from, and the scale factor that says how much bigger or smaller everything gets.

interaction.hint: Distances from the centre double when $k = 2$.

config.prompt: Drag the pink handle until $k = 2$. Centre stays at $(0, 0)$.
config.successText: $k = 2$: every distance from the centre doubled.

altExplain.prompt: Watch one corner while you drag: its distance from the centre gets multiplied by the scale factor. If the image sits on the opposite side of the centre, the scale factor must be negative.

interaction.hint: Every corner moves to one-and-a-half times its distance from the centre.

config.prompt: Scale by $k = 1.5$ from the centre at $(0, 0)$.
config.successText: $k = 1.5$. One and a half times as big as the original.

slides.title: Can scale factor be less than 1?

interaction.hint: Distances halve and the image gets smaller, but it's still called an enlargement.

config.successText: $k = \tfrac{1}{2}$ is an enlargement too. The word covers shrinking as well as growing.

interaction.hint: Lengths scale by $k$. Areas scale by $k^2$, so square the scale factor.

config.prompt: After an enlargement with scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$, the image area is...

options.whyWrong: Half is what happens to lengths. Areas use $k^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

options.text: one quarter of the object area

options.whyWrong: Only if $k = 1$. Here $k = \tfrac{1}{2}$, so area must change.

config.successText: Areas scale by $k^2$. $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}$. Volume would be $k^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}$.

altExplain.prompt: Think of a square. Side length $L$ becomes $kL$. Area was $L \times L = L^2$, now $kL \times kL = k^2 L^2$. So area multiplies by $k^2$, not by $k$. For $k = \tfrac{1}{2}$, area becomes $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of the original.

Watch corner $(5, 1)$: it swings up and over to $(-1, 5)$, which is against the clock.
Three quarter-turns anticlockwise equals one quarter-turn clockwise, and that lands the triangle below the axis.
A rotation about $(1, 1)$ would leave that point fixed and land the image somewhere else. Check with one corner.
$(-1, 2)$ is where a corner landed, not the point everything turned around.
